title: Layer 2/3 Pyramidal Cells
intro: Layer 2/3 pyramidal cells are the most numerous cells of the superficial cortex and its main link to other cortical areas. They receive feedforward input from layer 4, a dense web of recurrent input from each other, and feedback from higher areas on their apical tufts in layer 1. They fire sparsely, and their activity is where much of the cortex's learned selectivity is seen.

items: Morphology: a soma in layer 2 or 3, several basal dendrites, and an apical dendrite that rises to layer 1 and branches into a tuft. Cells in layer 2 have shorter apical trunks and wider tufts than those deeper in layer 3. Total dendritic length is a few millimetres in rodents and much more in humans, where layer 2/3 cells are larger and more complex (Mohan et al. 2015).

Inputs: layer 4 excitatory cells (feedforward), other layer 2/3 cells (recurrent, the largest single source), long-range cortico-cortical feedback on the tuft, higher-order thalamus in layer 1, and local PV, SST and VIP interneurons.

Outputs: axons to layer 5 (the strongest local projection, L2/3 to L5), to other layer 2/3 cells, and long-range intratelencephalic projections to other cortical areas, including the other hemisphere through the corpus callosum.
Firing: regular spiking with adaptation. Passive properties in rodent slices: resting potential near −70 to −80 mV, membrane time constant about 15 to 30 ms, input resistance roughly 50 to 200 MΩ.

Activity in vivo: very sparse. In mouse barrel cortex most layer 2/3 cells fire well below 1 Hz and many are nearly silent during whisking, while a small minority fires much more (Barth & Poulet 2012).

Connectivity: recurrent connections are not random. Cells with similar responses are more likely to connect and do so more strongly, forming clusters (Song et al. 2005; Ko et al. 2011; Cossell et al. 2015).

blocks.text: Thin basal and oblique dendrites of layer 2/3 cells can generate local NMDA spikes when a cluster of nearby synapses is active together (Schiller et al. 2000 showed this in layer 5; it has since been shown for layer 2/3 cells and in vivo, e.g. Smith et al. 2013 in mouse V1). The apical tuft receives feedback but is electrically far from the soma; in layer 2/3 the coupling is stronger than in the long layer 5 cells, and tuft input more readily affects firing directly. In human layer 2/3 cells, Gidon et al. (2020) found dendritic calcium-mediated action potentials whose amplitude is largest for threshold-level input and falls for stronger input, letting one dendrite compute an XOR-like function.

items: Detailed multi-compartment models: Blue Brain's L2 and L3 pyramidal m-types (L2_IPC, L2_TPC, L3_TPC) with fitted e-types (Markram et al. 2015); the Allen Institute's all-active models of mouse layer 2/3 cells (Nandi et al. 2022); human layer 2/3 models by Eyal et al. (2018), which show how large human dendrites keep distal synapses effective.

Point neurons: Izhikevich regular spiking (a = 0.02, b = 0.2, c = −65, d = 8) or the chattering preset for the subset that bursts rhythmically; AdEx with spike-triggered adaptation (Brette & Gerstner 2005 fitted their AdEx to a regular-spiking pyramidal cell model); Allen GLIF models fitted to individual mouse layer 2/3 cells (Teeter et al. 2018).

Network roles: in the Potjans-Diesmann (2014) microcircuit layer 2/3 is one LIF excitatory population of about 20,700 neurons, and its low rate (under 1 Hz) is reproduced by connectivity alone. In HTM, layer 2/3 is the 'output layer' that pools over sequences or objects (Hawkins et al. 2017).

blocks.text: Try it: a regular-spiking pyramidal cell

The AdEx neuron below starts with Brette and Gerstner's (2005) parameters for a regular-spiking pyramidal cell (spike-triggered adaptation b = 80.5 pA, adaptation time constant 144 ms). Watch the interspike intervals lengthen as the adaptation current w builds up. Set b to 0 and a to 0 and the adaptation disappears, which is what a plain integrate-and-fire neuron would do.
What this means for your SNN

items: Use an adapting regular-spiking model, not plain LIF; adaptation keeps rates low under sustained drive.
Expect and aim for sparse activity: a few per cent of cells active at a time, with heavy-tailed rates.
Make recurrent excitatory connections sparse, weak and learnable; like-to-like clustering emerges with STDP and is a check that learning works.
Give the cells a second, apical input if you want feedback or predictions to modulate them (see Layer 5 Pyramidal Cells for the strongest version of this).
